weaknesses: Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper says reward and implementation details are in an appendix, but no appendix is present. Exact reward definitions, weights, thresholds, token vocabulary, temporal resolution, architecture dimensions, group size, optimizer, training schedule, scenario sampling, compute, and random seeds are omitted.

The stated GRPO objective is technically underspecified and differs materially from standard clipped GRPO/PPO formulations: it uses an unclipped full-trajectory importance ratio and leaves the KL estimator undefined. The experiments do not isolate the claimed contributions. Consequently, the results establish that additional reward optimization helps, but not that GRPO or the dual-model design is responsible.

The closest cited approaches, Gen-Drive and TrajHF, are not evaluated directly. Comparisons appear to mix published systems with potentially different training data and pipelines, while the manuscript does not report repeated runs, uncertainty, significance, or sufficient simulator configuration details.

The frozen predictor is assumed to be a realistic reactive world model under counterfactual ego actions, but this is neither validated nor stress-tested. Long autoregressive rollouts can accumulate error or be exploited by the policy, and training with this learned model is mismatched to evaluation with IDM or log replay.

Several claims overreach the evidence. Claims that the method preserves diverse, human-like behavior are unsupported by behavioral-distribution or diversity metrics. Likewise, describing hand-designed rewards as unbiased and claiming strong generalization or real-world safety from one simulator benchmark are overstatements.

The central explanation of VD-GRPO is technically overstated. Subtracting each group's mean does not preserve absolute reward magnitudes across groups; it preserves within-group scale. The learned world model is never evaluated for prediction accuracy, calibration, responsiveness, or robustness under policy-induced distribution shift. It is trained with teacher forcing but rolled out autoregressively, while evaluation uses IDM agents. Downstream score improvements therefore do not demonstrate that it provides realistic interactions, and exploitation of model errors is not investigated.

The world-model ablation is interpreted misleadingly: the claimed +7.23 R-CLS benefit compares the complete RL system with the pretrained baseline and conflates several changes. The relevant reactive-world-model versus ground-truth-replay difference is only 2.60 points.

Evidence for safety is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Evaluation uses one simulator benchmark whose component metrics substantially overlap the training rewards, with no second dataset, out-of-distribution split, real-world study, collision counts or severity analysis, targeted rare-event evaluation, or failure-case analysis.

No results include independent seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or even evaluation sample counts. This is especially problematic for rare safety events and for several sub-point SOTA differences.

The SOTA claim is selective. With rule-based post-processing, Plan-R1 is worse than Diffusion Planner on both Test14-hard metrics and on Test14-random NR; without post-processing it is also worse on Val14 NR. Literature-sourced comparisons may additionally differ in training data, compute, and post-processing.

Important reproducibility details remain missing, including reward thresholds, overspeed normalization, planning horizon and agent selection, token clustering parameters, fine-tuning batch/update schedule, clipping behavior, scenario sampling, continuous-trajectory reconstruction, controller integration, and exact refinement/post-processing configuration. The paper lacks a limitations or safety discussion despite making strong claims about autonomous-driving safety. Simulation-to-real limitations, reward misspecification, world-model exploitation, and residual failure risks should be explicitly addressed.
